summary: The IETF normally meets in person three times a year, but events can make a planned meeting infeasible. This Best Current Practice gives criteria to help the IETF LLC, the IESG and the IRTF Chair decide whether to relocate, virtualize, postpone or cancel an in-person meeting.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a big meeting can't happen where planned. This document helps leaders decide whether to move it, go online, delay it or call it off.

subtitle: How the IETF decides whether to move, virtualize, postpone or cancel an in-person meeting when events get in the way.

tldr.problem: The IETF normally holds three in-person meetings a year, but venue closures, disasters, war, health crises, economic shocks or visa changes can make a planned meeting infeasible.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF LLC judges whether the meeting is logistically and financially viable, the IESG and IRTF Chair judge whether attendance will be high enough, and four remedies are ranked from relocation down to cancellation.
tldr.outcome: A Best Current Practice that sets the decision criteria, the order of preference for remedies and when registration fees should be refunded.

facts.label: Emergency cutoff
facts.value: Within fourteen weeks of the meeting

facts.label: Postponement notice
facts.value: Start at least 30 days after announcement

facts.label: Relocation limit
facts.value: No new air travel less than one month before

today: RFC 9137 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 226) and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Meetings Might Not Happen
sections.content:
The IETF ordinarily holds three in-person meetings per year. RFC 9137 gives criteria for the case where a planned meeting becomes unsuitable, which may not be obvious right away.

The RFC lists example triggers: a venue that closes or cannot meet requirements, a natural disaster that degrades travel infrastructure, war, civil unrest or a public health crisis, an economic crisis that cuts travel budgets, and visa or government restrictions that shut out many attendees.
sections.eli5: A school trip can be ruined by a broken bus, a storm or a sick teacher. This document is about what to do when a big meeting hits that kind of trouble.

sections.title: Who Decides What
sections.content:
The work is split in two. The IETF LLC (IETF Administration LLC) assesses whether an in-person meeting is logistically and financially viable and gathers information on travel restrictions. The IESG and the Chair of the IRTF assess whether projected attendance is sufficient for a viable meeting.

The RFC uses RFC 2119 keywords as defined in BCP 14, and uses the word venue to mean both the session facility and the official hotels, as defined in RFC 8718.
sections.eli5: One group checks whether the building, money and travel can work. Another group checks whether enough people will show up to make it worthwhile.

sections.title: The IETF LLC and Emergency Criteria
sections.content:
If a major event happens more than fourteen weeks before the meeting starts, it is a non-emergency situation. Later events, up to and including the meeting week, are emergencies. In a non-emergency where the meeting clearly cannot proceed, the IETF LLC MUST share its reasons with the community and MUST consult on its proposed remedy. In less clear cases it SHOULD run a formal reassessment: consult on the timetable and criteria, publish an assessment report and recommended remedy, and seek approval from the IESG and IRTF Chair.

In an emergency there is no time for consultation, so the IETF LLC MUST apply criteria with IETF consensus: local safety guidelines allow the meeting, Internet access can be provisioned (including native IPv4 and IPv6 and redundant paths), enough food and drink is within walking distance, and local health and safety services can cope with the visitors. It MUST also assess the effect on its own operations, such as available staff and the financial impact. It SHOULD cancel an in-person meeting that is logistically impossible or inconsistent with its fiduciary responsibilities.
sections.eli5: If there is lots of warning, the organizers ask everyone for ideas. If the trouble comes at the last minute, they use a ready-made checklist: is it safe, is there Internet, is there food, and can the town handle it?

sections.title: Judging Attendance
sections.content:
If the IETF LLC finds no fundamental obstacles in an emergency, the IESG and the IRTF Chair decide whether projected attendance is high enough to gain the benefit of meeting in person. They SHOULD cancel the in-person meeting if that benefit is insufficient.

They are discouraged from relying on a simple head count, since even dramatically smaller meetings with large remote participation may succeed. They might ask whether many working groups and research groups are largely unaffected, and whether there is a critical mass of key personnel at most working group meetings.
sections.eli5: It is not just about counting heads. A smaller party can still be great if the right people are there and others join online.

sections.title: The Four Remedies
sections.content:
Remedies are weighed against four principles, in no particular order: hold the scheduled sessions in some format, provide the benefits of in-person interaction when possible, avoid exorbitant extra travel costs, and leave enough time and resources to prepare an alternative. They are listed in approximate declining order of preference.

  • Relocation: keep the meeting week but move to a more accessible venue, geographically close if possible. The IETF LLC SHOULD meet the criteria in RFC 8718 and RFC 8719, and relocation needing new air travel SHOULD NOT happen less than one month before the start.
  • Virtualization: make the meeting fully online. This needs different processes that are outside this document's scope.
  • Postponement: delay to a specific date at the same venue. The meeting MUST begin no earlier than 30 days after the announcement, and must end at least 30 days before the next IETF meeting begins. A meeting can be both postponed and relocated, with the drawbacks of both.
  • Cancellation: possible when worldwide conditions make even online attendance hard. It can affect the nomination process and the seating of new officers, and is likely the only option for emergencies right before or during a meeting.
sections.eli5: Best choice is to move the party to a nearby place. Next is to hold it online. Then comes delaying it. Last is calling it off.

sections.title: Refunds
sections.content:
The IETF SHOULD NOT reimburse unrecoverable travel expenses such as airfare and hotel deposits. Registration fees are treated differently:

  • Cancellation SHOULD give a full refund to all participants, which MAY be prorated if some sessions finished without incident.
  • On postponement, the IETF LLC SHOULD offer refunds to those who cannot attend at the new time, and attendees can opt out of a refund.
  • On virtualization, the IETF LLC MUST offer the difference between the paid fee and the online-meeting fee, and SHOULD offer refunds to those who do not wish to attend online.
  • It SHOULD offer refunds to attendees whose government forbids or advises against visiting the venue, even if the meeting goes ahead, but SHOULD NOT refund cancellations due to employer policy or personal risk assessments.

These provisions aim to maintain trust, but the IETF LLC may suspend them under extraordinary threats to the organization's solvency.
sections.eli5: If the party is cancelled, you get your ticket money back. You usually do not get back money for a plane ticket you already bought.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The RFC states that it introduces no new concerns for the security of Internet protocols, and that it has no IANA actions. For situations it does not foresee, the IETF LLC should protect the health and safety of attendees and staff and the fiscal health of the organization, with approval from the IESG and the IRTF Chair, and the IESG should pursue a later update of the document.
sections.eli5: Nothing here changes how the Internet works. If something surprising happens, leaders should keep people safe and the money healthy.

viz.caption: REMEDIES IN APPROXIMATE ORDER OF PREFERENCE

cells: Same week, nearby venue; no new air travel less than one month before
Fully online; processes out of scope
Start at least 30 days after announcement; end at least 30 days before next meeting
When even online attendance is hard, or emergency leaves no time
